title: Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum
summary: Approximately 56 million years ago, a massive and geologically rapid release of thousands of gigatons of carbon triggered the Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum. Global temperatures surged by 5 °C to 8 °C, accompanied by widespread ocean acidification and deoxygenation, causing major benthic foraminiferal extinctions, mammalian dwarfism, and polar migrations. The event serves as the primary deep-time geological analog for understanding the long-term planetary consequences of modern anthropogenic greenhouse emissions.

uncertainty.note: Onset placed at c. 55.9–56.0 Ma; the main carbon injection and recovery phase lasted approximately 100,000 to 200,000 years.

where.modern_name: Global atmosphere and oceans (worldwide planetary event)
where.historical_name: Global ocean-atmosphere system during the Paleocene–Eocene transition; no human polities existed

importance.justification: The most prominent Cenozoic hyperthermal event, driving global ocean acidification, benthic extinctions, and major evolutionary turnover in mammals and plants.

related.because: The end-Cretaceous extinction ten million years earlier cleared ecological space for the Cenozoic mammalian radiations that diversified during the PETM.

beats.caption: Massive carbon injection into the atmosphere triggers rapid global heating and ocean acidification.
Widespread extinction of benthic marine organisms coincides with mammalian dispersals toward the poles.
